items.q: Match the following insulin regimen — 1) Basal-bolus 2) Premixed 3) CSII (pump) 4) Twice-daily NPH … A) Long-acting basal + rapid bolus B) Fixed-ratio biphasic insulin C) Continuous subcutaneous infusion D) Conventional older regimen
items.exp: Basal-bolus uses long-acting basal + rapid bolus; premixed is fixed-ratio; CSII is continuous infusion; twice-daily NPH is the older conventional regimen. (Book p932)

items.q: A T1DM patient has fasting hyperglycaemia on NPH and normal pre-dinner glucose. The next step is:
opts: Review 3 a.m. glucose to distinguish dawn phenomenon from Somogyi
Switch to insulin glargine without evaluation
items.exp: Differentiating dawn phenomenon (high 3 a.m. and fasting) from Somogyi (low 3 a.m., high fasting) requires a 3 a.m. glucose check before changing regimen. (Book p932)

items.q: Assess dawn vs Somogyi: I Dawn phenomenon is treated by increasing night-time insulin. II Somogyi is treated by reducing night-time insulin.
items.exp: Dawn phenomenon is treated by increasing basal insulin; Somogyi is treated by reducing night-time insulin to avoid nocturnal hypoglycaemia. (Book p932)

items.q: Which is the odd one out — a long-acting basal insulin?
items.exp: Insulin aspart is a rapid-acting analogue; the others are basal analogues. (Book p932)

items.q: The page's '8-8-8 + 16 U' overlap regimen at diagnosis of T1DM combines morning split doses with evening ___.
items.exp: An 8-8-8 short-acting insulin plus 16 U basal insulin covers meals and overnight; this split-mixed regimen allows individual titration. (Book p932)

items.q: Match the following rapid-acting insulin analogue — 1) Lispro 2) Aspart 3) Glulisine … A) Rapid-acting B) Rapid-acting C) Rapid-acting
items.exp: Lispro, aspart and glulisine are all rapid-acting analogues; differences are in excipients and onset (typically 5–15 min). (Book p932)

items.q: A T1DM patient has recurrent nocturnal hypoglycaemia on NPH. The most appropriate change is:
opts: Switch to insulin detemir or glargine with dose titration
items.exp: Recurrent nocturnal hypoglycaemia warrants switching from NPH to a flatter basal analogue such as detemir or glargine. (Book p932)

items.q: Assess CGM: I CGM reduces hypoglycaemia in T1DM. II CGM is not indicated in T2DM.
items.exp: CGM reduces hypoglycaemia in T1DM and increasingly is used in insulin-requiring T2DM as well. (Book p932)

items.q: Match the following SMBG / CGM measure — 1) 6-point profile 2) Time in range 3) Glycaemic variability 4) GMI … A) Pre- and post-meal + bedtime B) Percentage 70–180 mg/dL C) Standard deviation / coefficient of variation D) Glucose management indicator from CGM
items.exp: 6-point profile covers pre/post meals and bedtime; TIR is the percentage in 70–180 mg/dL; glycaemic variability uses SD or CV; GMI is the CGM-derived HbA1c estimate. (Book p932)

items.q: A T2DM patient on basal insulin has TIR 80% with low glucose events. The most appropriate next step is:
opts: Maintain current regimen and review CGM data
items.exp: TIR 80% with no/low hypoglycaemia is generally considered good control; maintain and review. (Book p932)

items.q: CGM-derived HbA1c estimate is called the ___.
items.exp: GMI is the CGM-derived estimate of HbA1c; it is useful when laboratory HbA1c is unreliable. (Book p932)

items.q: Assess adjustments: I +2 / −4 rule (printed) increases dose if above target by 2 units. II Insulin detemir can be dosed twice daily.
items.exp: Page-print +2/−4 is a titration rule for above/below target; detemir is often twice daily because of slightly shorter duration than glargine. (Book p932)
